transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been concerning you?

Well, doctor, my wife actually pushed me to come in. What really brought me here is that she'll be talking to me, telling me about my cousin's appointments or who needs a ride where, and I'm looking right at her, but... a minute later I realize I didn't actually take in half of what she said. It's causing some friction, and I figured I should get it checked out.

When your wife is talking to you and you're looking at her, are you thinking about other things at that moment, or does it feel like your mind just goes blank—like you're not really 'there' even though you're looking at her?

I'm honestly not sure. I don't know if I'm actively thinking about something else, or... if my mind just sort of empties out. It's hard to pin down. 

I just know that I'm looking right at her, and I hear her speaking, but the actual meaning of what she's saying just doesn't register. I couldn't tell you exactly where my head goes in those moments.
How long has this been happening—are we talking about the past few weeks, months, or has this been going on for years?

Well, it's been going on for a while, but it's definitely been noticeably harder for about 11 months now. That's when my cousin moved in with us after having surgery. It seems like since then, there's just been a lot more to keep track of, and I'm struggling with it more.

Besides conversations with your wife, do you notice this difficulty paying attention happening in other situations too—like at work, while reading, or in other conversations—or is it mainly when she's talking to you?

It definitely happens in other situations, yeah. It's not just with her. Like, um... if I sit down to work out a catering order, or if I'm listening in on a parish planning call. I usually start off fine, but before long my mind just wanders off. I end up having to go back over the exact same notes because it's like I never even read them the first time.
Besides having trouble focusing, do you find yourself feeling restless, fidgety, or like you need to move around? Or do you tend to act on impulses without thinking things through?

No, I wouldn't say so. I don't really feel restless, and I'm not... I don't fidget or feel like I need to be up and moving around all the time. Sitting still is perfectly fine for me. 

And as for acting on impulses, no, that doesn't really sound like me either. I don't just jump into things without thinking. It really is just the trouble paying attention that I'm dealing with.
Over these past 11 months or so, have you been feeling persistently sad, down, or depressed most days? Or have you noticed a loss of interest in things you normally enjoy?

No, I wouldn't say I've been feeling sad or depressed. I mean, it's been a little stressful with everything going on, but my mood is generally fine. And I still enjoy doing the things I usually do, like volunteering at the church and all that. It's really just the focus issue that's bothering me.

When you're doing something you really enjoy—like volunteering at church or a hobby—do you still have this trouble focusing and your mind wandering, or does it seem to happen mainly when you're dealing with tasks that feel more demanding or stressful?

I haven't really noticed it happening with the things I enjoy. If I'm doing hands-on volunteer work at the church or something I really like, I usually stay on track just fine. It definitely seems to happen mostly with the more demanding or tedious stuff—like I mentioned, looking at those catering numbers or just sitting and listening to a long call. That's when my mind really starts to wander.

Going back further—did you have trouble concentrating or focusing on tasks like schoolwork when you were younger, say in school or as a teenager? Or is this attention problem something that's really only started becoming noticeable in adulthood?

Well, no, it's not just a recent thing. Even way back in grade school, definitely before I was twelve, I had those same kinds of issues. I remember my teachers telling my parents that I was a bright kid, but that I was just always daydreaming. I would... I'd leave my finished homework sitting right there in my desk, or the teachers would have to keep reminding me to actually finish my classwork. So, yeah, it's been a problem for a long time.

You mentioned your teachers had to remind you to finish classwork and you'd leave homework in your desk—did these attention issues back then actually affect your grades or cause problems for you in school, or were you still able to do okay academically despite the daydreaming?

I actually did okay academically, for the most part. I mean, my grades weren't terrible. It was mostly just the teachers constantly having to redirect me or point out that I wasn't paying attention. But I still managed to pass my classes and get by alright.
When you were in grade school, did your parents or family members also notice this daydreaming and difficulty paying attention at home, or was it mainly something your teachers saw at school?

I'm not really sure, to be honest. It's been a long time, but... I don't really remember my parents making a big deal out of it at home. It seemed like it was mostly just the teachers bringing it up. If my folks noticed me daydreaming around the house, they didn't really say much about it that I can recall.

When you were younger in grade school, besides the daydreaming your teachers mentioned, did these attention problems actually cause you trouble—like struggling to keep up with schoolwork, getting lower grades than you were capable of, or having difficulty completing assignments?

Well, like I mentioned a minute ago, it didn't really cause me that kind of trouble. My grades were always fine. I mean, maybe I could have gotten slightly better marks if I was paying full attention all the time, but I wasn't failing or struggling to keep up. 

The only real difficulty with the assignments was just... actually finishing them when I was supposed to, or remembering to hand them in. But it never really ruined my report card or anything like that.
Besides school, do you remember having trouble with attention or focus affecting other parts of your life growing up—like with chores at home, playing sports, or friendships with other kids?

No, not that I can remember. Like I said, my parents didn't really seem to notice much at home, so chores weren't really a big issue. And I didn't play sports or anything, so there wasn't a problem there. As for friends, I just hung out with the neighborhood kids like anyone else. I don't recall my attention causing any problems with them. It really just seemed to be a school thing.

You mentioned that since your cousin moved in about 11 months ago, the attention problems have gotten noticeably worse. Before that time, even though you had the daydreaming issue back in school, were you able to manage your work and daily responsibilities pretty well, or had the attention problem been causing you real difficulties in your job or personal life for years?

Before my cousin moved in, I managed things fine, honestly. It really wasn't causing me any problems for years. But lately, it's... well, it's started causing some actual tension at home. My wife feels like she just can't count on me with my cousin's care because I keep losing track of what I'm doing. 

And with the catering I do, I've had to constantly double-check myself or even redo tasks just so the small jobs don't get mixed up. So, yeah, the real difficulties have definitely just been over these last eleven months or so.

Around the time your cousin moved in 11 months ago, or in the months leading up to that, did you experience any head injuries, serious infections, illnesses, or did you start taking any new medications? Or have you had any medical problems that a doctor diagnosed during that time?

No, nothing like that. I haven't had any head injuries or bad infections, and I'm not on any new medications. I haven't been diagnosed with any new medical problems either. It's just been the stress of having him move in, I think.
Have you noticed any other changes in your health over the past 11 months—like changes in your sleep, energy level, weight, or how you physically feel—besides the attention problems?

No, not really. My sleep is fine, and my weight hasn't changed or anything. I mean, my energy is about the same as it always is. Physically, I feel fine, honestly. It's really just the focus issues we've been talking about.

When your mind wanders or you're not fully present during conversations or tasks, do you ever feel disconnected from your surroundings, or like you're watching yourself from outside your body, or like things around you don't feel quite real?

No, I don't feel anything like that. I don't feel disconnected or like I'm watching myself. Things feel real enough, I just... I just lose my train of thought or get distracted. It's not like an out-of-body thing at all.

When your mind wanders during a conversation or task, does your wife or anyone else ever notice that you seem to blank out or stare off into space for a bit—like you're not responding to them for a few seconds or a minute—or do you stay responsive and aware of what's going on around you the whole time?

No, I don't blank out or stare off like that. My wife hasn't mentioned anything like that either. I'm still responsive, I just... I might ask her to repeat what she said because I wasn't really listening, but I'm not frozen or anything. I'm fully aware of what's going on around me.

Has your wife or anyone else ever noticed you having episodes where you suddenly seem unaware or unresponsive for a few seconds to a minute or two—like you're not reacting to them or what's happening around you—even if you don't remember it happening?

No, she hasn't ever mentioned anything like that. Like I said before, I don't really freeze up or stop responding. I'm just easily distracted. But nobody has ever told me I have episodes where I'm completely unresponsive.
